title: Mars Has a Hidden Temperature Divide Inside It
hook: The southern half of Mars's interior may run hundreds of degrees hotter than the north — hot enough to be partly molten, and enough to explain several Martian puzzles at once.
key_points: Analysis of Mars's interior finds a large-scale thermal asymmetry between its northern and southern hemispheres.
The southern interior could be hundreds of degrees hotter than the north, and partially molten.
A partly molten region behaves differently for seismic waves, which fits observed patterns in marsquake data.
The divide may also explain Mars's unusual crustal magnetism, which is far stronger in the south.
A hotter southern interior bears on where liquid water could have persisted in Mars's past.
content_html: Mars looks lopsided from orbit — the southern highlands are ancient, cratered and elevated, while the northern lowlands are smoother and younger. Researchers now report that the split may run far deeper than the surface: the planet's southern interior appears to be hundreds of degrees hotter than its northern counterpart, hot enough in places to be partially molten.
extra_html:
The evidence comes from how Mars transmits seismic energy. Partly molten rock slows and damps seismic waves differently from solid rock, so marsquake signals crossing a hot region carry a distinguishable fingerprint. Modeling the planet's interior with that asymmetry built in reproduces observed seismic behavior better than a uniform interior does.

If the divide is real, it ties several loose ends together. Mars has no global magnetic field today, but its crust is magnetized — and far more strongly in the south, which a hemispheric difference in thermal history could account for. It also matters for water: a warmer interior means heat flowing up toward the surface for longer, which affects where liquid water could have persisted underground as the planet's surface froze. The result reframes Martian geophysics around a planet that has been thermally two-faced for most of its existence.

related.title: Venus May Be Tearing Itself Apart From Within
related.hook: Venus was long filed away as a geologically dead world. New 3D simulations say its giant rift valleys are young — and may still be pulling open.

related.title: Solving Saturn's Spin Mystery
related.hook: Saturn's measured spin rate kept drifting, baffling astronomers for decades. The James Webb telescope reveals the planet wasn't speeding up — its winds were fooling us.

related.title: Why Some Giant Planets Spin Faster Than 'Failed Stars'
related.hook: Astronomers clocked the spins of dozens of distant worlds and found a surprise: lightweight giant planets can twirl faster than the much heavier brown dwarfs — so mass isn't the whole story.

flashcards.prompt: What did researchers find about the inside of Mars?
flashcards.back_html: A hemispheric temperature divide: the southern interior may run hundreds of degrees hotter than the northern one, and may be partially molten.

flashcards.prompt: How can seismic data reveal a partially molten interior region?

choices.text: Seismic waves travel differently through partly molten rock than through fully solid rock
Molten rock emits its own seismic waves that detectors pick up directly
Molten regions block all seismic waves completely, leaving a silent zone

flashcards.explanation_html: Wave speed and attenuation depend on the material's state. Marsquake signals passing through a partly molten region carry a distinguishable signature, which is what makes the thermal divide detectable from the surface.

flashcards.prompt: Which Martian mysteries might a hot southern interior help explain?
flashcards.back_html: The planet's unusual crustal magnetism, which is concentrated in the south; puzzling patterns in its seismic behavior; and where liquid water could have survived in its ancient past.
